thread.title: Earnings worries weigh on Asian markets - MarketWatch

author: Lucy Craymer
title: Earnings worries weigh on Asian markets - MarketWatch
text:
11:43 p.m. ET Share 
Samsung falls on outlook uncertainty; AMA, Nomura drag Nikkei AFP/Getty Images Samsung Galaxy Note 8 smartphones are displayed at the company's showroom in Seoul on Wednesday. 
By Lucy Craymer 
Stock indexes in Japan and South Korea suffered earnings-related hits Friday, with Samsung Electronics falling 3.5% after rival Apple’s latest quarterly financial results. 
Apple AAPL, +0.21% reported a slight drop in iPhone sales in the three months through December and gave a downbeat revenue forecast for the current quarter. Its shares still rose 3.4% in after-hours trading as the tech giant’s overall results beat expectations and because the stock‘s performance had been lackluster for several months on worries about demand for the iPhone X. 
Samsung 005930, -3.73% has its own line of smartphones but also makes various phone components including chips and screens. “The market is concerned about the uncertainty” surrounding Samsung’s outlook, said S.K. Kim, an analyst at Daiwa Capital Markets. Chip maker SK Hynix 000660, -2.82% dropped 2.5%, contributing to the Kospi’s SEU, -1.66% 1.5% decline. 
Japan’s Nikkei Stock Average NIK, -0.91% , which jumped 1.7% a day earlier, fell 1.3% by the midday break following earnings-related news. Airline ANA Holdings 9202, -3.71% and investment bank Nomura Holdings 8604, -3.44% reported results after the bell, and their shares were off 4.2% and 3.6%, respectively. 
As for Thursday’s jump, “I think the market got carried away” since some other indexes were down, said Michael McCarthy, CMC Markets’ chief market strategist in Australia. 
Chinese stocks SHCOMP, -0.41% were down 0.4% midday, extending the previous day’s decline, while Hong Kong’s stock benchmark HSI, -0.01% erased an early 1% drop to trade flat at the midday break. 
Big-cap stocks started strongly this year in China, ”so we have not been surprised to see some profit-taking this week,” said David Millhouse, head of China research and strategy at Forsyth Barr Asia. He added that concerns about high levels of leverage in the market and local reports of possible new moves by regulators to reduce debt has put pressure on stocks. 
In addition, the People’s Bank of China has drained money from the financial system via open-market operations for six consecutive days. 
In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 XJO, +0.47% climbed 0.3%, boosted by a 1.9% jump in the energy sector, putting that group on pace for its best day in three months. 
Oil futures were higher with the U.S. benchmark up 0.5% at $66.14 a barrel, poised to notch a fresh three-year settlement high. ANZ Bank said the market’s focus has returned to the positive macroeconomic backdrop, looking past record levels for U.S. oil production. 
Some investors were likely sidelined ahead of Friday’s U.S. jobs report and as government-debt yields continued to rise. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield nearly reached 2.8% in Asian trading and was at four-year highs. 
“Equity markets globally are becoming aware that bond yields are increasing, and ultimately that means scope for rate hikes” and stimulus efforts unwinding, said Stuart Ive, senior client manager at OM Financial. “These moves in the bond market might start to get investors a bit twitchy.” 
Bitcoin prices BTCUSD, -5.63% remain below $9,000, according to CoinDesk, after first breaching that level in U.S. trading Thursday for the first time in more than two months. Prices are 13% below day-earlier levels for the volatile cryptocurrency. Related Topics
